title: Geospatial Indexing
subtitle: Watch a ride app find the nearest drivers by turning 2D space into cells it can look up directly.
learn: Why latitude and longitude do not work well with ordinary indexes
How geohash turns a location into a string whose prefix means 'same box'
How a quadtree adapts to crowded and empty areas
What S2 and H3 cells add, and why you search a cell plus its neighbours
How a live driver index is kept fresh and queried in a few milliseconds

steps.title: Who is closest to me?
steps.body: A rider taps 'request ride' at one point in a city. About 200,000 drivers are online in the metro area, each one a latitude and longitude that changes every few seconds. The app must return the 5 closest available drivers in well under a second. How do you search positions without checking every driver?
steps.idea: Proximity search asks for everything near a point, and a point has two coordinates, not one.
steps.caption: A rider asks for nearby drivers.

steps.title: The naive scan
steps.body: The simplest answer computes the distance to every driver and sorts. That is 200,000 distance calculations per request. An ordinary B-tree index on latitude does not rescue you: it narrows only one axis, to a long stripe across the whole city, and you still filter the rest. Even a composite (lat, lon) index narrows well only on the first column. Real databases ship spatial indexes (PostGIS uses an R-tree, a tree of nested bounding rectangles; Redis GEO uses geohash). The next steps show the cell-based idea. Assume the full scan costs roughly 400 ms, which is too slow at thousands of requests per second.
steps.idea: A one-dimensional index cannot answer a two-dimensional 'nearby' question efficiently.
steps.caption: Scanning every driver takes about 400 ms.

steps.title: Geohash: space as a string
steps.body: Geohash repeatedly halves the map, alternating longitude and latitude, and writes the result as a short string such as 'tdr1v9'. Points in the same box share the same prefix. At 6 characters a cell is roughly 1.2 km by 0.6 km; at 7 it is about 150 m square. Now 'nearby' becomes an ordinary lookup: fetch the drivers stored under the rider's cell key. Here that returns 14 drivers instead of 200,000, and an in-memory index answers in about 4 ms.
steps.idea: Geohash turns a 2D position into a string key, so a plain key lookup or prefix scan finds a neighbourhood.
steps.caption: Look up one cell key, not every driver.

steps.title: The boundary problem
steps.body: A rider standing at the edge of a cell may have the closest driver just across the line, in the next cell with a completely different prefix. A shared prefix guarantees nearness, but a different prefix does not mean far away. The standard fix is to query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours (9 cells, about 60 candidates here), then compute exact distances on those few results. Pick a cell at least as wide as the distance you care about. If you get fewer than 5 candidates, widen to the next ring of cells.
steps.idea: Cells are a coarse filter: search the cell and its neighbours, then rank by exact distance.
steps.caption: Query 9 cells, get a short candidate list.

steps.title: Quadtree: cells that adapt
steps.body: A quadtree starts with the whole map as one box. Whenever a box holds more than a set number of points, say 100, it splits into four children, and so on. Dense downtown ends up in tiny boxes while an empty suburb stays one big box. Lookups descend the tree. The catch: it usually lives in memory on one node, and moving drivers mean constant inserts and removals. It has the same edge problem too, so you also read neighbouring leaves. Here we count a leaf plus 4 adjacent leaves (5 cells).
steps.idea: A quadtree splits only where data is dense, so every leaf holds a similar number of points.
steps.caption: The tree descends to a small leaf box.

steps.title: S2 and H3: cells on a sphere
steps.body: Flat grids distort near the poles. Google's S2 maps the globe onto a cube and orders cells along a space-filling curve (a path that visits every cell while keeping neighbours close in order), so each cell is a single 64-bit id and nearby cells get nearby ids. Uber's H3 uses hexagons, whose 6 neighbours are all the same distance away, which makes 'rings' of cells simple. H3 resolution runs 0 to 15, higher meaning smaller hexagons; at resolution 8 a hexagon is about 0.7 square km. A hexagon plus one ring is 7 cells.
steps.idea: S2 and H3 are geohash's idea done on a sphere: fixed ids per cell, with cheap neighbour and ring lookups.
steps.caption: Search the rider's hexagon plus one ring of neighbours.

steps.title: Keeping drivers fresh
steps.body: Each driver app sends a GPS ping every 4 seconds, so 200,000 drivers produce about 50,000 writes per second. Pings go onto a stream, and an updater reads them. On every ping it refreshes the driver's last-seen time, a cheap in-memory write. It moves the id between cell sets only when the driver crosses into a new cell. A periodic sweep (or a per-driver key with a TTL, time to live) drops anything not refreshed within about 30 seconds, so offline drivers disappear on their own. The latest coordinates also go to the driver store (a key-value store handles this rate, or you can batch writes).
steps.idea: Refresh last-seen on every ping, move cell membership only on a cell change, and let stale entries expire.
steps.caption: Pings refresh the driver; a cell change moves the id.

steps.title: Rank and answer
steps.body: With about 60 candidate ids in hand, the service loads each driver's current coordinates, rating and availability from the driver store. It computes the true distance, drops anyone who is busy or too far, sorts, and returns the top 5. The cell lookup shrank 200,000 drivers to a few dozen, so the expensive exact work runs on almost nothing. The 12 ms here is the cell lookup plus loading 60 rows.
steps.idea: Two phases win: a cheap cell filter to shortlist, then exact math on the shortlist.
steps.caption: Shortlist, exact distance, top 5 back.

steps.title: A stadium empties
steps.body: Fixed-size cells assume roughly even density. After a concert, 5,000 drivers pile into a single cell, so one lookup returns a huge list while the quiet cell next door is empty. Assume a lookup of that size takes about 60 ms. Fixes: use a finer resolution where cells are busy, let a quadtree split that area, or cap the shortlist per ring and expand outward in distance order only if you need more.
steps.idea: Uneven density breaks fixed cells; go finer or adaptive in hot spots.
steps.caption: One hot cell returns thousands of ids.

steps.title: From 200,000 to a few dozen
steps.body: Proximity search is hard because 'near' is two-dimensional. Geohash, quadtrees, S2 and H3 all map space to cells so that a lookup replaces a scan. Usually you search the cell plus its neighbours, then rank by exact distance. Keep the index in memory, update it only when a driver changes cell, and choose the cell size to match how crowded the area is.
steps.idea: Index space as cells, shortlist by cell and neighbours, then rank exactly.
steps.caption: Cells turn a scan into a lookup.

quiz.q: Why can't a plain B-tree index on latitude alone make 'drivers within 2 km' fast?
options: It indexes the longitude axis only
It narrows only one axis, leaving a long stripe of rows to filter by longitude
It would need one index per driver
It only works for exact matches
quiz.why: A latitude range selects a band across the whole city. The longitude condition still has to be checked row by row inside it, so the index helps far less than for a one-dimensional query.

quiz.q: A rider sits right on the edge of a geohash cell. What query avoids missing the closest driver?
options: Search only the rider's own cell with a longer prefix
Retry with a shorter hash only if the first result is empty
Search the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours, then sort by exact distance
Sort all drivers by their geohash string
quiz.why: Nearby points can fall in different cells. Reading the neighbours covers drivers within about one cell width, and exact distance on the small shortlist picks the closest of them.

quiz.q: Which situation most favours a quadtree over fixed-size cells?
options: A dense downtown next to large empty areas
Drivers spread evenly across a flat plain
Needing a 64-bit id per location
Storing the index only on disk
quiz.why: A quadtree splits only where points are dense. Fixed cells are either too coarse downtown or needlessly many in sparse areas; a quadtree gives each leaf a similar number of points.

quiz.q: Drivers ping every 4 seconds, yet a driver moves between cell sets far less often. Why?
options: Pings are dropped at random
Cells are recomputed once per hour
Riders update the index instead
Most pings keep the driver in the same cell, so only a last-seen refresh is needed
quiz.why: A cell is roughly 150 m to a kilometre wide, so most pings leave the driver in the same cell. The updater just refreshes last-seen and moves set membership only on a cell change, which keeps index churn low.

quiz.q: After a concert, one cell returns 5,000 candidates and queries slow down. What is the most sensible response?
options: Use a coarser cell size everywhere
Use finer cells or an adaptive split in that hot area
Remove the neighbour lookup
Move the index to disk
quiz.why: The cell is too coarse for that density. A finer resolution or a quadtree split keeps the shortlist small where the crowd is, without changing quiet areas.

cheatsheet.def: String encoding of a location from interleaved lat/lon bits. Longer string means smaller box; a shared prefix means the same enclosing box.
Close points can sit in different cells. Query the cell plus its neighbours, then rank by exact distance.
Recursive 4-way split of the map, splitting a box only when it holds too many points. Adapts to uneven density.
Google's library: sphere mapped to a cube, cells ordered along a Hilbert curve (a space-filling curve that keeps neighbours close in order), each cell a 64-bit id with 31 levels.
Uber's hexagonal grid with 16 resolutions (0 to 15; higher means smaller hexagons). Every neighbour is equidistant, so ring and distance queries are simple.
Use cells as a cheap coarse filter to shortlist tens of candidates, then compute exact distance on just those.
Rule of thumb: pick a size that holds tens of results, not thousands. Go finer in dense areas, widen rings in sparse ones.
